meta.tagline: A car-free village, glacier trains and the Matterhorn's shadow

pills: The Matterhorn: the world's most famous peak

overview.title: Welcome to Zermatt
overview.intro: Zermatt resembles a devotion built around a single mountain: the Matterhorn's crooked pyramid stands at the end of every street, opposite every balcony, in the corner of every photo. Petrol cars cannot enter the village — electric mini-taxis hum past, skiers walk from the railway station to the pistes, and centuries-old blackened wooden barns stand among the boutique hotels. In winter it is one of the world's highest ski regions; in summer a paradise of trails. The moment the peak sheds its cloud, every head in the village turns the same way — yours will too.

local_word.definition: The Matterhorn's name in the local Valais dialect: villagers call their mountain 'ds Horu' — 'the Horn'. A Zermatter's question 'is the Horu out?' is the national weather bulletin that sets the day's plan.

rules.title: Set the summit hour for morning
rules.description: The Matterhorn often puts on its cloud cap in the afternoon: the odds of a clear view are highest in the morning. Put Gornergrat and the photo plans early — leave the afternoon to the village and valley.

rules.title: Respect the altitude, trust the layers
rules.description: The village sits at 1,600 metres, the summit stations at 3,000-3,900: the altitude is felt and the weather turns in minutes. Climb slowly, drink water, never skip sunscreen — mountain sun burns twice as hard off the snow.

rules.title: Leave the car at Täsch
rules.description: Private cars cannot enter Zermatt: drivers park at the Täsch terminal and ride the 12-minute shuttle train down. Luggage trolleys roll right onto the train — the system works flawlessly; don't fight it.

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: The Gornergrat railway is the best box seat

tip.label: The Zermatt philosophy
tip.text: In this village plans are made by the Horu: if the peak is out, drop everything and go up; if it's hidden, it's museum, spa and fondue hour. The mountain's calendar outranks yours — accept it, relax.

transport.title: Around Village and Mountain
transport.intro: Zermatt's transport is three-dimensional: streets on foot, valleys by train, summits by cable car — all running like a watch.

items.title: Arriving — via Visp and Täsch
items.description: The main line connects at Visp to the mountain railway; drivers park at the Täsch terminal and board the 12-minute shuttle. From the Geneva-Zurich direction, the whole journey rewards with scenery.

items.title: The Gornergrat railway — an open-air box seat
items.description: The cog railway, running since 1898, climbs from the village to 3,089 metres: sit on the right, and the Matterhorn fills the window all the way. At the top, a glacier amphitheatre and 29 four-thousanders await.

items.title: The Matterhorn Glacier Paradise chain
items.description: The cable car chain rises to Europe's highest cable station (3,883 m): a glacier palace, summer skiing and the view into Italy. The Crystal Ride cabins' glass floors are a courage bonus.

items.title: The village on foot + e-taxi
items.description: The main street (Bahnhofstrasse) walks end to end in ten minutes; hotels ferry guests in electric minibuses. Listen to the silence — instead of engines you hear hooves and the rush of the stream.

items.title: Trails and winter footpaths
items.description: 400 km of summer trails and groomed winter walking paths: the Sunnegga funicular is the gate to the five lakes route, the Furi cable car to the glacier gorge. The trail signage is Swiss-standard flawless.

callout.label: Train tip
callout.text: Take the first train up the Gornergrat and walk a leg down, getting off at Riffelberg or Rotenboden: the paths descending along the line give twice the ticket's worth of views. The Rotenboden-Riffelsee descent is the official route of the reflection photo.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Zermatt the question is a balcony question: a façade facing the Horu, the sound of the stream, or the piste's edge?

local_word.definition: The Valais's blackened wooden grain barns: centuries-old structures standing on stone discs to keep the mice out. They still stand in rows along the Hinterdorf lane — the village's oldest photo studio is right there.

items.name: Bahnhofstrasse and the centre
items.description: On and around the main street: walking distance to the station, the lifts and the restaurants. Lively in ski season, après-ski soundtrack included — the location makes everything easy.

items.name: Around the Hinterdorf
items.description: The quarter of centuries-old wooden barns: old Zermatt's fabric, stone roofs and silent lanes. Two minutes to the centre, two centuries back in atmosphere — for waking up inside history.

items.name: The Matterhorn side — south balconies
items.description: Hotels and chalets with balconies facing the Horu: open the curtains and the peak stands opposite your bed. The price multiplies with the view — most people come to Zermatt once, and stay here.

items.name: Winkelmatten
items.description: The village's upper quarter: chalet lanes, family guesthouses and shortcuts to the pistes. A five-to-ten-minute walk to the centre — for seekers of the calm + ski balance.

items.name: Täsch
items.description: The terminal village down the valley: prices markedly friendlier, Zermatt 12 minutes by shuttle train. The sensible choice for drivers and for those saving the budget for mountain tickets.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Zermatt is a two-season stage: a ski cathedral in winter, a trail paradise in summer; the in-betweens are quiet, but the peak never leaves.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Spring Snow and the Low Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Skiing up high, first green below
items.description: Spring snow is skied on the high pistes into late April; May-June is the breathing-space season — some lifts close for maintenance, prices soften, and the lower trails open.

callout.label: June tip
callout.text: Come in June: the meadows in flower, the streams loud with meltwater, the village calm. High trails may hold snow patches — pick routes by the opening report; the tourist office keeps it current.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Peak Trail Season
items.subtitle: Summer · 400 km of trails, lake reflections
items.description: The heart of the hiking season: the five lakes route, the glacier gorges and Europe's highest summit stations run at full capacity. Mornings are clear, afternoons build cloud — the early riser wins.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: Take the first train towards Riffelsee: before the wind rises, the Matterhorn's reflection sits mirror-still on the lake. After 10, wind and crowds both spoil it — this photograph's shift is 8 am.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Golden Larches
items.subtitle: Autumn · Yellow larch forests, crystal summits
items.description: September-October is Zermatt's hidden masterpiece: the larch forests turn gold, the air sharpens to crystal, the trails empty. The first snow powders the summits — photography's most generous season.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In early October walk the Sunnegga-Findeln line: golden larches, blackened chalets and the snowy Horu in one frame. Findeln's mountain restaurants have season-end calm — tables with views, bookings easy.

items.label: Winter
items.name: The Ski Cathedral
items.subtitle: Winter · 360 km of pistes, skiing into Italy, après-ski
items.description: The vast three-sector ski area links to Italy's Cervinia: the altitude guarantees snow and the season runs long. The village glitters and prices peak — New Year and February school weeks sell out months ahead.

callout.label: Season note
callout.text: Lock the winter holiday early: New Year and the February half-term fill months in advance. Never go off-piste without a guide — the glacier zone's rules are strict, and their reasons are serious.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Valais cooking is the mountain's cooking: melted cheese, air-dried meat, rye bread and the wine of Europe's highest vineyards.

local_word.definition: The Valais pie whose name frightens and whose self charms: potato, leek, apple and cheese in one pastry. It takes its name from the epidemic days when it was made from whatever was in the house — history's most delicious necessity.

items.name: Raclette du Valais — in its homeland
items.description: You're in raclette's motherland: the wheel's face is melted at the fire, scraped over potatoes, balanced with pickles. In the village restaurants the 'AOP Valais' mark is the seal of the real thing.
items.tag: In its homeland · with the AOP seal

items.name: Fondue — the after-piste cauldron
items.description: The official close of a cold piste day: the pot in the middle, bread on the fork, white wine alongside. Whoever drops their bread in the pot has their forfeit decided at the table — the tradition is serious.
items.tag: After the piste · pot in the middle

items.name: Walliserteller — the dried meat platter
items.description: Beef air-dried in mountain air, smoked ham, alpine cheese and rye bread: the Valais's charcuterie pride on one plate. The classic opener with a glass of Fendant.

items.name: The Cholera pie
items.description: The potato-leek-apple-cheese quartet in pastry form: found in mountain huts and village bakeries. Don't trip over the odd name — its sweet-savoury balance is surprisingly fine.
items.tag: Valais heritage · try it in a hut

items.name: Wine of the high vineyards — Heida
items.description: The Heida white from Europe's highest vineyards (Visperterminen, 1,150 m) and the Valais's Fendant: the mountain table's local glasses. 'Mountain wine' here is not marketing — it's geography.
items.tag: The local glass · from the high vines

items.name: The mountain hut break
items.description: Rösti, homemade tart and view-served hot chocolate in the trail-side huts (towards Findeln and Zum See): Zermatt's best lunch address is often at 2,100 metres. A sunny-terrace booking is essential in season.
items.tag: On the trail · on a sunny terrace

callout.label: Budget tip
callout.text: Zermatt's prices race its altitude: strike the balance with the bakery sandwich + supermarket picnic + one good dinner trio. The mountain-station self-services are markedly kinder than the restaurants too — same view, different bill.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone knows the Gornergrat; these six are Zermatt's quiet layers.

items.name: The Riffelsee reflection
items.description: Five minutes from Rotenboden station: on a windless morning the Matterhorn finds its twin in the lake. The photographers' dawn watch is here — join it on the first train, then walk down to Riffelberg.

items.name: The Hinterdorf lane
items.description: Two steps behind the main street, blackened barns and stone-disc granaries: the village's pre-tourism self is frozen here. When the lanterns come on at dusk, the lane becomes a time machine.

items.rarity: The memory of the mountain's price
items.name: The Mountaineers' Cemetery
items.description: In the churchyard rest the climbers who gave their lives to the Matterhorn and the surrounding peaks — among them traces of the 1865 first-ascent disaster. The village's quietest, deepest corner.

items.rarity: A corridor carved by the glacier
items.name: The Gorner Gorge (Gornerschlucht)
items.description: The glacier-water canyon at the village's edge: wooden walkways hang above turquoise water. The half-hour loop is a cloudy afternoon's best plan B.

items.name: The Findeln hamlet
items.description: The old alpine hamlet on the path down from Sunnegga: blackened chalets, golden larches and mountain restaurants facing the Horu. Skiers in winter and hikers in summer meet on the same terraces.

items.name: The 5-Seenweg's quieter lakes
items.description: Stellisee is the five lakes route's star, but Grindjisee's larch frame and Leisee's swimming jetty escape most visitors: complete the route — every lake gives a different portrait of the Horu.

callout.label: Sunset tip
callout.text: In the evening light walk up from the village — to the church bridge or towards Winkelmatten: the pink blaze called alpenglow catches first the Horu's tip, then the whole wall. It lasts five minutes and stays a lifetime.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Zermatt is honest, but mountain tourism's price-and-expectation games apply here too.

items.name: Burning a summit ticket in cloud
items.description: Cable tickets are serious money; at a cloud-bound summit there is nothing to see beyond the glacier palace.
items.instead: Check the webcams in the morning (they run on every screen in the village): if the Horu is hidden, trade the day for gorge, museum, spa and fondue. The ticket won't run away — the cloud will.

items.name: Renting equipment without a plan
items.description: Whoever hunts ski equipment last-minute at season's peak pays the leftover price for the leftover sizes.
items.instead: Reserve equipment online in advance and ask for the multi-day discount. If you're a hiker, don't skimp on poles and boots — the trails are stony and knees come one per customer.

items.name: Every meal in the main-street window
items.description: Bahnhofstrasse's showcase restaurants run at tourist tempo: prices high, the kitchen sometimes average.
items.instead: Turn one lane in, or eat lunch in a mountain hut: the same budget buys both view and kitchen. For dinner, ask a local for their raclette address.

items.name: Underestimating the altitude
items.description: Whoever arrives from sea level and rides to 3,800 metres on day one meets headache and breathlessness; whoever leaves the marked route in the glacier zone takes a serious risk.
items.instead: Spend day one in the village and middle altitudes, climb gradually, drink plenty of water. Never leave the marked line in the glacier zone — those markers aren't decoration, they're insurance.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Zermatt the costliest mistake is haste and the best investment patience: save the summit for a clear day and the big spend for a planned choice. The Horu has stood four thousand years — it can wait out your two hours of flexibility.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order. (Summer version — in winter the piste replaces the trail.)

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A Horu day from reflection to alpenglow

steps.title: First train up the Gornergrat
steps.description: Sit at the right-hand window: the Horu keeps you company all the way. At the top, the glacier amphitheatre and 29 four-thousanders — breakfast on the terrace.

steps.title: The Riffelsee reflection
steps.description: Off at Rotenboden and five minutes to the lake: take the mirror shot before the wind rises, then walk the path down to Riffelberg.

steps.title: A hut lunch at Findeln
steps.description: Cross to the Sunnegga side; rösti + Heida on a Findeln chalet terrace: the view is on the menu.

steps.title: Leisee and the descent
steps.description: A courage swim or jetty pause at Leisee; descend by funicular or path and pass through the Hinterdorf's barn lane.

steps.title: The alpenglow watch
steps.description: Take your place at the church bridge: watch the Horu's pink blaze — the village's five quietest minutes.

steps.title: The fondue close
steps.description: Pot in the middle, Fendant alongside: the day is sealed Valais-style. Don't drop the bread — the forfeit gets discussed at the table.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Summits, lakes and glacier — the full Horu dose

steps.title: Classic Zermatt
steps.description: The one-day flow above: Gornergrat, Riffelsee, Findeln, alpenglow, fondue.

steps.title: The glacier world
steps.description: The cable chain to Matterhorn Glacier Paradise: the ice palace, the 3,883 m terrace and the view into Italy; a Furi pause + the Gorner Gorge walkways on the way down; raclette at night and a quiet moment at the mountaineers' cemetery.

steps.title: Five lakes and farewell
steps.description: Complete the 5-Seenweg: from Stellisee to Leisee, every lake a different Horu portrait; lunch in a hut, a spa hour or Bahnhofstrasse stroll in the afternoon; a farewell evening of Cholera pie + one last alpenglow.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: The Valais dialect is as solid as its mountains; these five open doors on trail and in hut alike.

items.meaning: Hello — everyone who meets on a trail greets; it's practically law
Thank you very much — works on the hut terrace too
Enjoy your meal — said as the fondue pot opens
Cheers! — eye contact as the Fendant rises
'The Horn' — the Matterhorn's local name; use it and the villagers smile
